_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 164 - George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before (Gutenberg #14224, London 1884): ch. 3 (religion/soul), ch. 4-5 (gods), ch. 18 (moon calendar), ch. 19 (origin of fire and other stories), ch. 20 (names of islands). Topics 2 deity narratives, 5 ritual origin, 8 trickster, 10 festival. All passages are labeled paraphrase; existing record polynesian-tiitii-fire covers the Ti'iti'i fire tale.

title.en: The Anganga and Pulotu, Land under the Ocean
title.zh: 靈魂安岡加與海底樂土普洛圖

region.en: Falealupo, west Savaii, and Pulotu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島法萊阿盧波與普洛圖（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (London 1884)

summary.en: Samoans believed in a soul, the anganga, which at death left the body and went to the hadean regions under the ocean, called Pulotu, entered from the neighbourhood of Falealupo at the western point of Savaii. Birth placed every Samoan under an aitu - a god who appeared in some visible incarnation: eel, shark, turtle, dog, owl or lizard. To eat the incarnation of one's own god was death, for the god would dwell in the body of the offender and generate there the very thing he had eaten.
summary.zh: 薩摩亞人信有靈魂安岡加——人死離體，前往海底冥府普洛圖，其門戶在薩瓦伊島西端法萊阿盧波附近。人皆有守護神艾圖：或顯於鰻、鯊、龜、犬、鴞、蜥；若人食己神之化身，神便入其腹中孕育其所食之物，至死方休。

sensitivity.note: Samoan eschatology and totemic belief summarized.

passages.text: The Samoans believed in a soul or disembodied spirit, which they called the anganga. Anga means to go or come, according to the particle of direction suffixed; the reduplicated anganga is used to designate the soul as distinct from the body, which at death was supposed to go away from the body and proceed to the hadean regions under the ocean, which they called Pulotu. At his birth a Samoan was supposed to be taken under the care of some god, or aitu, as it was called: the help of several of these gods was probably invoked in succession on the occasion, and the one who happened to be addressed just as the child was born was fixed on as the child's god for life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: These gods were supposed to appear in some visible incarnation, and the particular thing in which his god was in the habit of appearing was to the Samoan an object of veneration - in fact, his idol, and he was careful never to injure it or treat it with contempt. One saw his god in the eel, another in the shark, another in the turtle, another in the dog, another in the owl, another in the lizard, and so on throughout all the fish of the sea, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things; in some of the shell-fish even, gods were supposed to be present. A man would eat freely of what was regarded as the incarnation of the god of another man, but the incarnation of his own particular god he would consider it death to injure or to eat. The god was supposed to avenge the insult by taking up his abode in that person's body, and causing to generate there the very thing which he had eaten, until it produced death. This class of genii, or tutelary deities, they called aitu fale, or gods of the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Village God and the Oath of the Coconut Cup

region.zh: 薩摩亞村廟（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (London 1884)

summary.en: Every village had its god; every child born there was 'his property'. The temple might hold a conch shell blown to rouse the village to war, a sacred cup, or stones; the cup served in oaths - hands laid upon it: 'With my hand on this cup, may the god look upon me, and send swift destruction, if I took the thing which has been stolen' - and before this ordeal the truth was rarely concealed. Village gods were incarnate in owl, heron, bat or rainbow; a dead owl found on the road was wept over, the forehead beaten with stones till blood flowed, and the bird buried like a human body - while its flight in war was omen and command.
summary.zh: 各村皆有其神；村中新生嬰兒皆屬其所有。廟中或懸海螺——神欲開戰便吹之；或懸椰殼聖盃，用以起誓：『手按此盃，願神鑒察，若竊物者是我，願遭天誅。』臨此神判，真相極少能藏。村神或顯於鴞、鷺、蝠、虹；路遇死鴞，村民當場痛哭，以石擊額至血流，鄭重如葬人；而戰時鴞翔之向即進退之令。

sensitivity.note: Samoan communal religion; blood-mourning described as recorded practice.

passages.text: Another class of Samoan deities may be called gods of the town or village. Every village had its god, and every one born in that village was regarded as the property of that god: a woman would say on the birth of her child, 'I have got a child for so-and-so', and name the village god. There was a small house or temple also consecrated to the deity of the place; where there was no formal temple, the great house of the village, where the chiefs were in the habit of assembling, was the temple for the time being. Some settlements had a sacred grove as well as a temple, where prayers and offerings were presented.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: In their temples they had generally something for the eye to rest upon with superstitious veneration. In one might be seen a conch shell suspended from the roof in a basket made of cinnet network, and this the god was supposed to blow when he wished the people to rise to war; in another, two stones were kept; in another, something resembling the head of a man, with white streamers flying, was raised on a pole at the door of the temple on the usual day of worship; in another, a cocoa-nut shell drinking-cup was suspended from the roof, and before it prayers were addressed and offerings presented. This cup was also used in oaths: if they wished to find out a thief, the suspected parties were assembled before the chiefs, the cup sent for, and each would approach, lay his hand on it, and say, 'With my hand on this cup, may the god look upon me, and send swift destruction, if I took the thing which has been stolen.' The stones and the shells were used in a similar way. Before this ordeal the truth was rarely concealed: they firmly believed that it would be death to touch the cup and tell a lie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The village gods, like those of the household, had all some particular incarnation: one was supposed to appear as a bat, another as a heron, another as an owl. If a man found a dead owl by the roadside, and if that happened to be the incarnation of his village god, he would sit down and weep over it, and beat his forehead with stones till the blood flowed - this was thought pleasing to the deity. Then the bird would be wrapped up and buried with care and ceremony, as if it were a human body; this, however, was not the death of the god, who was supposed to be yet alive, and incarnate in all the owls in existence. The flight of these birds was observed in time of war: if the bird flew before them, it was a signal to go on; but if it crossed the path, it was a bad omen and a sign to retreat. Others saw their village god in the rainbow, others in the shooting star; and in time of war the position of a rainbow and the direction of a shooting star were always ominous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Young Maui of Savage Island Steals the Fire

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Three hundred miles south of Samoa, the natives of Savage Island have a somewhat similar tale about the origin of fire: instead of Talanga and Ti'iti'i they give the names of Maui the father and Maui the son; instead of going through a rock their entrance was down through a reed bush; and instead of a stipulation for the fire, the youth Maui, like another Prometheus, stole it, ran up the passage, and before his father could catch him had set the bush in flames in all directions. The father tried to put it out but in vain - and ever since the exploit of young Maui they have had fire and cooked food in Savage Island.
summary.zh: 薩摩亞以南三百里的紐埃島（野島）流傳著同源異文之火源神話：主人翁換作父子雙毛伊；入口不在岩縫而在蘆叢之下；取得之途亦非談判，而是竊取——小毛伊如另一普羅米修斯，攜火而逃，尚未被父追及便將蘆叢四處點燃；父親撲火無功。自從小毛伊這番功業之後，野島之人便有了火與熟食。

sensitivity.note: Fire-theft cluster: Niue Prometheus variant of the Ti'iti'i story.

passages.text: The natives of Savage Island, 300 miles to the south of Samoa, have a somewhat similar tale about the origin of fire: instead of Talanga and Ti'iti'i, they give the names of Maui, the father, and Maui, the son; instead of going through a rock, their entrance was down through a reed bush. And, instead of a stipulation for the fire, they say that the youth Maui, like another Prometheus, stole it, ran up the passage, and before his father could catch him, he had set the bush in flames in all directions. The father tried to put it out, but in vain; and they further add, that ever since the exploit of young Maui, they have had fire and cooked food in Savage Island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wars of Stones, Grass and Trees

region.zh: 薩瓦伊島高地（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: A golden age when all things spoke and warred: small stones beaten by grass, grass by bush-grass, bush-grass by trees, trees by creepers - 'and then began the wars of men'. The fish beat the birds in their first battle, fish becoming birds; the birds beat the fish in the second and have reigned ever since. The bat borrowed the rat's wings and never returned them; the banana family, beaten by the plantain, hangs its head in defeat - while the erect plantain remains the symbol of its own victory.
summary.zh: 太古黃金時代，萬物能言能戰：石敗於草，草敗於叢草，叢草敗於樹，樹敗於藤——『然後人類的戰爭開始了』。魚首戰勝鳥，魚化為鳥；再戰鳥勝，鳥遂永掌天翼。蝙蝠借鼠之翼而不還；芭蕉族敗於山蕉，從此垂首示敗——山蕉依然昂首，是自身勝利的標記。

sensitivity.note: Cosmogonic battle sequence; Turner's remark that these may encode inter-village wars noted.

passages.text: The Samoans have their stories of a golden age of intelligence long long ago, when all things material had the power of speech. They not only spoke, but they had evil natures as well, and quarrelled with each other and fought, very much like the races of mankind. To give it in their own words: 'The small stones fought with the grass, the stones were beaten and the grass conquered. The short grass fought with the strong weedy grass, the short grass was beaten and the strong grass conquered. The strong grass fought with the long grass of the bush, the strong grass was beaten and the bush grass conquered. The bush grass fought with the trees, the grass was beaten and the trees conquered. The trees fought with the creepers, the trees were beaten and the creepers conquered - and then began the wars of men.' The principle seems to be that whenever one thing prevails to excess above another thing, be it rock, stone, earth, grass or tree, we are sure to find some tradition of its battle and victory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: A story is told of a battle between two trees - a Fijian Banian tree and the Samoan tree called Tatangia. A report reached Samoa that the trees of Fiji had fought with the Banian tree and that it had beaten them all; on this the Tatangia and another tree went off from Samoa in two canoes to fight the Fijian champion. They reached Fiji, went on shore, and there stood the Banian tree. 'Where is the tree which has conquered all the trees?' 'I am the tree', said the Banian. 'I have come to fight with you.' They fought: a branch of the Banian tree fell, but Tatangia sprung aside and escaped; another fell - ditto - the Tatangia; then the trunk fell, and again Tatangia darted aside unhurt. On this the Banian tree 'buried its eyes in the earth' and owned itself conquered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: There were also accounts of battles fought by the birds on the one side and the fish on the other: the fish and the birds were in the habit of paying friendly visits to each other. The inanga, or small fry of a fresh-water fish, were offended at not being hospitably received on shore by the birds; on the other hand the birds despised the inanga for being so small. They fought, and the fishes conquered, and it ended in the fish becoming birds and the birds fishes - hence they say the back-bone of the inanga projects so much. But after that there was another battle, in which the fish were beaten and the birds conquered; and ever since the birds have had their wings, and their supremacy, and the right of going to the sea or the river as they please to pick up the fish which come within their reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that the rat had wings formerly, and that the large bat or flying fox at that time had no wings. One day the bat said to the rat: 'Let me try on your wings for a little, that I may see how I like flying.' The rat lent the bat his wings; off flew the bat with the wings and never came back to return them - hence the proverb applied to a person who borrows and does not return: 'Like the bat with the rat.' With the exception of the mountain plantain all the bananas have their bunches of fruit hanging downwards towards the earth like a bunch of grapes; the plantain shoots up its bunch of fruit erect towards the heavens. As the reason of this we are told that of old all the bananas held their heads erect, but they quarrelled with the plantain, fought, were beaten, and ever since have hung their heads in token of their defeat, whereas the plantain is erect still, and the symbol of its own victory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Tasi the Last Becomes First: The Owl, the Serpent, the Ten Brothers
title.zh: 貓頭鷹、蛇與十兄弟：末位成首位

region.zh: 薩瓦伊島林間（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Ten brothers named after the numerals - Sefulu first, Tasi last - go to the forest for canoe timber and find an owl and a serpent fighting. Nine refuse the owl's plea; Tasi alone takes up his felling axe and kills the serpent. 'Well done, Tasi! To keep in remembrance your bravery, you shall stand foremost in everything that is numbered: Sefulu who has been first shall now be last, and you who have been last shall always be first.' So Samoan counting runs Tasi, Lua, Tolu... to Sefulu.
summary.zh: 十個以數字命名的兄弟入林伐舟材，遇貓頭鷹與蛇相鬥。九位兄長皆推卻鴞的求援；唯有末弟塔西掄斧斃蛇。鴞曰：『幹得好，塔西！為永誌你的勇氣，萬物計數你當居首：原為第一的塞福魯降居末位，而原居末位的你永為第一。』薩摩亞數數至今自塔西起、以塞福魯終。

passages.text: A battle also between the owl and the serpent is noteworthy. There were ten brothers, whose names were Sefulu, Iva, Valu, Fitu, Ono, Lima, Fa, Tolu, Lua, and Tasi, and so named from the ten numerals, which in those days began with Sefulu as 1 and ended with Tasi as 10. These ten brothers went to the forest to cut wood for a large canoe; they came upon an owl and a serpent fighting. Sefulu was walking first, and to him the owl called out: 'Sefulu, you come and kill my enemy here, the serpent, and if you do you shall have a right to the Ifilele and Maota timber trees.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'No, let us pass on', said Sefulu, 'there are plenty of other trees which will answer our purpose.' Then the owl turned to Iva and all the others on to Lua, and implored help in killing the serpent, but each in turn answered as did Sefulu. Tasi, however, replied to the entreaty of the owl, and said, 'Yes, I will', and grasping his felling axe struck out at the serpent and killed it. 'Well done, Tasi!' said the owl, 'and to keep in remembrance for all time to come your bravery and respect for me, you shall stand foremost in everything that is numbered. Sefulu who has been first shall now be last, and you who have been last shall always be first.' And so it has continued to the present day - the first, Tasi, and the tenth, Sefulu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Toa and Pale: The Tree That Kept Rising
title.zh: 托阿與帕萊：砍而不倒的兄弟樹

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Fleeing the cannibal king of Fiji, brothers Toa and Pale become trees. Pale takes the crooked creeper-covered shape and begs Toa to do the same; Toa stands erect as a handsome straight tree - and the king's carpenters, seeking a keel, choose him. Cut down, he is raised again by Pale; the cutting, falling and rising goes on till nightfall, when they give up. 'What a Toa I have been to you!' says the felled one - and Samoans still say, when one has been a burden to another, 'What a Toa it has been to you!'
summary.zh: 為避斐濟食人王，兄弟托阿與帕萊化為樹。帕萊化作纏藤的歪樹，勸弟從同；托阿偏要挺立如良材——造舟匠果然相中，揮斧砍伐；倒下即被帕萊扶起，砍倒又起，直至入夜作罷。托阿嘆道：『我真成了你的托阿（拖累）！』——至今薩摩亞人仍說：『你真是我的托阿。』

passages.text: The King of Fiji was a savage cannibal, and the people were melting away under him. Toa and Pale were brothers; they wished to escape being killed for the oven, and so fled to the bush and became trees. It was only the day before a party were to go to the woods to search for a straight tree from which to make the keel of a new canoe for the king. They knew this, and so Pale changed himself into a crooked stick overrun with creepers, that he might not be cut by the king's carpenters, and advised Toa to do the same; he declined, however, and preferred standing erect as a handsome straight tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The party in search of a keel went to the very place, liked the look of Toa, and decided to cut it down. They cut, and Toa was felled to the ground, but Pale, who was close by, immediately raised him up again. The carpenters were confounded - cut again - but it was just the same. They persevered, and the cutting, falling, and rising again went on till night fell, when they gave it up. After they left Toa said to Pale, 'What a Toa (trouble) I have been to you!' - and hence the proverb to this day, when a person or thing has been a trouble to another, he says to the sufferer in a sympathising or apologetic tone: 'What a Toa it has been to you!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fowl and the Turtle at the Cool Spring

region.en: Rocks above a spring, Upolu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏波盧島泉邊岩（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: The fowl claims the cool spring by the rock; the turtle, fresh from the hot salt sea, bathes and is driven off - 'Let whoever is first here in the morning have the spring'. The turtle toils all night up the river; the fowl, sure of one bound of her wings, roosts till sunrise - and finds the turtle before her. 'Here comes the fowl, the turtle is before you!' - the Samoan proverb for the lazy and the late.
summary.zh: 母雞霸佔清泉，海龜自滾熱鹹海而來只圖一浴，被逐出——『明晨誰先到，泉歸誰』。海龜連夜溯河而至；母雞自恃一躍即達，安睡至日出——泉邊早有海龜候著。諺云：『母雞來了，海龜卻已在前！』——薩摩亞人譏懶惰遲到者之辭。

passages.text: Take the story of the fowl and the turtle. A fowl made her headquarters over a rock from which a cool spring of fresh water ran out into the adjacent stream. One day a turtle made its appearance; it was enjoying the cool fresh bath, and rising now and then to look about, when it was addressed roughly by the fowl: 'Who are you?' 'I am a turtle.' 'Where have you come from?' 'From the hot salt sea.' 'What are you doing here?' 'Bathing, and enjoying the fine cool fresh water.' 'Be off, this is my water.' 'No, it is mine as much as it is yours.' 'Well, then', said the fowl, 'let us decide in this way which of us will have it: let each of us go away, and whoever is first here in the morning shall have the right to the spring.' 'Let it be so', said the turtle, 'I'm off to the briny sea; you go away to the village.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle was back from the sea, up the river, and at the spring very early in the morning. The fowl thought there was no need to hurry, as she could with one bound on her wings be at the rock, and so she roosted till the sun was rising, and then flew over to the rock; but there was the turtle before her! 'You are there, I see', said the fowl. 'Yes, I am', replied the turtle, 'and the spring is mine.' And hence the proverb applied to the lazy and the late: 'Here comes the fowl, the turtle is before you!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rat, the Octopus, and the Owls

region.zh: 薩瓦伊島海岸（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: A rat, a snipe and a crab build a canoe; a squall upsets it, and the exhausted rat rides on the octopus's back, drinking salt water and secretly gnawing the neck of his rescuer. Ashore, the pain reveals the treachery; the octopus summons his friends the owls, who hunt down the rat and eat him - hardly a morsel each, they were so many. 'Do not be like the rat with the octopus: evil will overtake you if you do.'
summary.zh: 鼠、鷸、蟹同造獨木舟；風暴覆舟，力竭的老鼠攀上章魚之背，一邊飲鹹水解渴，一邊暗中啃咬恩人頸項。登岸後劇痛揭穿背叛；章魚召集盟友群鴞，追獵群鼠而食之——鼠眾太多，每鴞分得寥寥。諺云：『莫效章魚背上的老鼠——忘恩者必遭惡報。』

passages.text: There were three friends, a rat, a snipe, and a crab. They thought they would like to look about them on the sea, and so decided to build a canoe and go out on a short cruise. They did so, and when the canoe was ready off they went: the snipe pulled the first paddle, the crab the second, and the rat steered. A squall came on, and the canoe upset; the snipe flew to the shore, the crab sank and escaped to the bottom, and the rat swam. The rat was soon fatigued, but an octopus came along, and from it the rat implored help. 'Come on my back', said the octopus. The rat was only too happy to do so. By-and-by the octopus said: 'How heavy you are! my back is getting painful.' 'Yes', said the rat, 'I drank too much salt water when I was swimming there; but bear it a little longer, we shall soon be at the shore.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the octopus reached the shore off ran the rat into the bush. The octopus felt the pain still, however, and now discovered that the rat had been gnawing at the back of its neck. The octopus was enraged, called all his friends among the owls to assemble, and begged them to pursue and destroy the rat. They did so, caught it, killed it, and ate it, but there was hardly a morsel for each, they were so many. And hence the proverb in exhorting not to return evil for good: 'Do not be like the rat with the octopus, evil will overtake you if you do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Sons of Pulotu and the First War
title.zh: 普洛圖四子與第一場戰爭

region.zh: 自普洛圖至帕帕特亞（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (London 1884)

summary.en: At Pulotu lived Head of Day and Tail of Day, whose four children - Rain, Long-grass, Heavens and Story - visited Papatea in the east. Ua was struck on the neck (hence taua, to beat the neck, the word for war); Fan's neck was trodden; Langi was spat upon; Tala escaped. Elo, king of Pulotu, made the first war in history and swept Papatea clean: the refugees Tutu and Ila gave Tutuila its name, U and Polu that of Upolu, Sa and Vaila Savaii - islands born of a massacre's survivors.
summary.zh: 普洛圖住著『晝之首』與『晝之尾』夫婦，四子雨、長草、天與故事東訪帕帕特亞，遭毒打羞辱——烏阿被打頸（戰爭一詞tauua即『擊頸』之源），凡被踏頸、天被唾面，唯故事全身而退。普洛圖王埃洛怒而興師，史稱第一戰，掃滅帕帕特亞：逃亡者圖圖與伊拉合名圖圖伊拉，烏與普魯合名烏波盧，薩與瓦伊拉合名薩瓦伊——群島之名竟生於屠戮之餘燼。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenesis legend naming the Samoan islands.

passages.text: Of the group generally it is said that a couple lived at Pulotu called Head of Day and Tail of Day; they had four children - Ua, or Rain; Fan, Long grass; Langi, Heavens; and Tala, or Story. The four went to visit Papatea. Pulotu is in the west, Papatea in the east. The Papateans heard of the arrival of the four brothers and determined to kill them: first Ua was struck on the neck, and hence the word taua, or beat the neck, as the word for war - this was the beginning of wars. Others stood on the neck of Fan, and hence the proverb in war: 'To-morrow we shall tread on the neck of Fan.' Others surrounded and spat on Langi, and hence the proverb for ill-usage or rudely passing before chiefs: 'It is spitting on Langi.' Tala was spared, and escaped uninjured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tala and Langi returned to Pulotu and told about their ill-usage. Then Elo, the king of Pulotu, was enraged and prepared to go and fight the Papateans; this was the first war in history. They went, they fought, they conquered, and made a clean sweep of Papatea - and hence the proverb: 'Like the rage of Elo.' All who fled to the bush were sought and killed; only those who fled to sea escaped: a man called Tutu and his wife Ila reached the island of Tutuila and named it so by the union of their names; U and Polu reached Upolu, hence the name of that island by uniting their names; Sa and Vaila reached Savaii, united their names also and, for the sake of euphony, made it Savaii instead of Savaila.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Brothers Who Weep January's Storms
title.zh: 一月風暴：哭泣的兩兄弟

region.zh: 薩摩亞天空（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (London 1884)

summary.en: January is Utu-va-mua, first yam-digging - or the two brothers Utuvamua and Utuvamuli, beaten in the war in heaven, who fled to earth bringing the January storms; or, escaping earth's wars to the skies, they look down on the hills - heaps of slain covered over with earth dug from the valleys - and their weeping and wailing and maddening exasperation occasion the storm and the hurricane. The Palolo worm swarms from the reefs three days a year, timed by the last quarter of the October moon.
summary.zh: 一月名『首掘薯』；又一說謂其源自烏圖瓦穆阿與烏圖瓦穆利兩兄弟：天界戰敗逃至人間，帶來一月風暴；或謂二兄避人間之戰而上天，俯瞰那些以谷土覆蓋的山丘——盡是陣亡者之墳——悲泣哀號、憤懣瘋狂，遂起風暴颶風。而每年有三天，帕洛洛蠕蟲自礁石湧出，其期由十月下弦月推定。

passages.text: This month, January, was called Utu va mua, first yam digging, and so named from their then digging wild yams before the cultivated ones were ripe. Others say that the origin of Utu va mua was in two brothers, the one called Utuvamua and the other Utuvamuli, who, when there was war in heaven, and their party beaten, fled to the earth and brought the January storms with them. A third account says that Utuvamua was the elder brother and Utuvamuli the younger, and that during a great war on earth they escaped to the heavens; that the hills are the heaps of slain covered over by earth dug up from the valleys, and that when the two brothers look down upon them their weeping and wailing and maddening exasperation occasion the storm and the hurricane. The month was also called Aitu tele, great god, from the principal worship of the month.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: July was called Palolo mua, the first of Palolo - the first month of the half year called the Palolo season. Palolo is that singular worm which swarms out from certain parts of the barrier reefs for three days in the course of a year, of which the natives are very fond, and all the more so from its rareness. If the last quarter of the moon is late in October, palolo is found the day before, the day of, and the day after, that quarter; if the last quarter of the moon is early in October, palolo does not come till the last quarter of the November moon. The middle day is the principal day for gathering these swarms of marine worms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (1884); not verbatim.
